entries.title: Italian at a glance
body: Italian is a Romance language, the national language of Italy and an official language of Switzerland. The verb ending usually makes the subject pronoun unnecessary: parlo already means “I speak”.
Almost every word ends in a vowel. A written accent marks stress on a final vowel: città, caffè, è.

entries.title: How Italian is spelled
entries.body: Spelling is close to the sound. c and g are hard before a, o, u (casa, gatto) and soft before e and i (cena “chay-na”, gelato). ch and gh keep them hard (che, ghiaccio). gn is like the ny in “canyon” (gnocchi). Double consonants are held longer: note the difference between note and notte.

entries.title: il, lo, la, and un, uno, una
entries.body: The article agrees with the noun and with the sound that follows. il and un are the ordinary masculine forms. lo and uno are used before s + consonant, z, gn, ps and a few others. gli is the plural of lo.

entries.title: essere, avere, and -are verbs
entries.body: essere and avere are irregular. Most verbs you learn first end in -are and follow parlare. The h in ho, hai, ha and hanno is silent; it keeps those words distinct from o, ai and a.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: The teens are regular from undici onward except for the spelling of sedici. venti drops the final vowel before uno and otto: ventuno, ventotto. Age uses avere: ho vent'anni.

entries.title: Please, thanks, and the bill
entries.body: grazie is “thank you”, prego answers it and can also mean “please” or “go ahead”. per favore is the ordinary “please”. The restaurant bill is il conto.

entries.title: tu and Lei
entries.body: tu is for friends, family and people your own age once you know them. Lei (written with a capital) is the polite “you”, with the same verb forms as “she”. In shops and with strangers, Lei is the safer start.
